content_voiceover: This page reviews two board exam questions on high risk AML genetics. The first asks which alterations are commonly seen in therapy related AML, and the answer includes all four listed findings, loss of chromosome five, loss of chromosome seven, TP53 mutations, and complex karyotypes, since therapy related AML classically carries these adverse cytogenetic and molecular changes after prior chemotherapy or radiation exposure. A key teaching point noted here is that under current risk models, adverse risk cytogenetic abnormalities occurring alongside an NPM1 mutation now override the otherwise favorable NPM1 signal and push the patient into the adverse risk category. The second question presents a sixty year old woman with prior breast cancer treated with mastectomy and adjuvant therapy, who develops AML with a translocation between chromosomes 11 and 23 producing a KMT2A rearrangement, plus an NPM1 mutation and a FLT3 internal tandem duplication. The correct answer identifies this as AML with an ICC defining recurrent genetic abnormality, since the KMT2A rearrangement itself is a defining lesion regardless of the treatment history or the co-occurring NPM1 and FLT3 mutations.
keypoints: Therapy related AML: -5, -7, TP53, and complex karyotype are all classic adverse findings
Adverse cytogenetics plus NPM1 mutation now defines adverse risk, not favorable
KMT2A rearrangement is an ICC AML-defining recurrent genetic abnormality
Prior cancer treatment history alone does not override a defining genetic lesion
keypoint_voiceover: Remember, therapy related AML shows -5, -7, TP53 mutation, and complex karyotype together. And when adverse cytogenetics coexist with NPM1 mutation, the case is now classified as adverse risk. Also, a KMT2A rearrangement is itself an ICC defining lesion, regardless of treatment history.
